title: Philistia
capsule: Philistia was the coastal polity of the Philistines, Sea Peoples who settled the southern Levantine coast around 1175 BCE following the Bronze Age collapse and organized themselves around the five city-states of Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron (Tel Miqne), and Gath — the Pentapolis. At their twelfth- and eleventh-century BCE apogee the Philistines possessed superior iron technology and dominated the Shephelah and coastal plain, defeating the Israelite confederation at Aphek (c. 1050 BCE) and capturing the Ark of the Covenant. David's campaigns (c. 1000–990 BCE) reduced Philistia to a vassal dependency, and Neo-Assyrian kings Tiglath-Pileser III and Sargon II further subjugated it in the late eighth century; Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed Ashkelon in 604 BCE and deported its population, ending organized Philistine political identity. Archaeological excavation at Tel Miqne-Ekron has revealed Aegean-style pottery and an Iron Age I industrial olive-oil complex illuminating Philistine material culture.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The five Philistine cities are well identified archaeologically; the territorial boundaries of the Philistine polity between the cities shifted over the attestation period and are reconstructed from biblical, Assyrian, and Egyptian texts combined with settlement surveys.
